title: ICE data recipes from Big Local News
text:
Preface

The Data Deportation Project
Big Local News has partnered with the Deportation Data Project to provide local reporters with simplified datasets and story recipes that can help them mine the millions of records of immigrants caught in the immigration enforcement system.
The Deportation data project, run by Graeme Blair of UCLA and David Hausman of Berkeley Law, began suing the federal government for individual level records about a decade ago and finally won access to some of the desired datasets, which they now make available to anyone on their website. The project is actively updating information from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. (Customs and Border Patrol, or CBP, has not yet provided data that is compatible with the ICE data, and the immigration courts run by the Justice Department provide completely different datasets, which haven’t yet been analyzed or cleaned by the project.) As of this writing, the project publishes data for arrests, detentions and detainers through October 2025, and is trying to get the agency to correct its recent releases on removals and encounters.
Each update to the data generally requires another lawsuit by the project, which means there is no standard release schedule even though the courts have ICE to produce the files.
These datasets are large and complex. For example, there are more than 300,000 people covering about xxx arrests in the arrest data alone. Detentions – people held in ICE facilities – cover xx million individual detentions, as the federal government moves people from place to place.
Big Local News is helping reporters in two ways. First, this guide provides step-by-step instructions for using the data posted on the DDP website. In addition, we have simplified some of the datasets to directly contribute to common story recipes without the need to deal with every column and every row provided in the original data. But every story idea can’t be boiled down to simple instructions. We encourage you to contact us for help when you have a story idea that might come from these records.


Credits
Reporters are in debt to the staff and law firms associated with the Deportation Data Project, especailly David Hausman and Graeme Blair, for all they have done to acquire, understand and share their data. We also thank all of the reporters who gave us important insights and story ideas, who are credited throughout this document.
Big Local News is responsible for any errors or omissions.

title: Immigration data ecosystem
text:
Alternative data sources
The Deportation Data Project is one of several major efforts at documenting arrests, detentions and removals in the immigration system. Before you delve into working on your own, consider whether some of these other sources might provide what your story needs.
One of the easiest parts of this complex data system to understand is the portion that tracks arrests, which refer to those arrests conducted by and in conjunction with ICE. (Notably, arrests effectuated entirely by Customs and Border Patrol are probably missing from these arrest data.) However, it’s not as straightforward to identify arrests that occurred by locality, or the specific criminal background of each person.
This reporting recipe will go through several scenarios for typical local stories, including how to search the Deportation Data project’s own site as well as how to use some enhanced and simplified data compiled by Big Local News.
It might not be necessary for you to do the work yourself! Before delving into a difficult data project, consider using these other efforts:

title: Immigration data ecosystem
text:
Relevant Research
Relevant Research aims to help academics analyze data for their work. The company is led by Austin Kocher, a Syracuse University researcher, and Adam Sawyer, formerly of the Transaction Records A?? Clearinghouse.1 Kocher often provides additional datasets on his Substack, such as his state-by-state arrest trends produced during his his initial review of the December 2 release of ICE data by DDP.
The immigration enforcement dashboard provides summary data on arrests and detainers, which you can filter by state. It lets you download monthly totals for your filtered data.
The detainer data on that site can also be filtered by state, and lists the 10 most common facilities that have detainers from ICE.
Another site by Relevant Research is its ongoing analysis of detention facilities owned and operated by ICE. This is a subset of the actual locations of detentions.


Vera Institute Detention trends
The Vera Institute provides analysis of each detention facility owned, operated or contracted by ICE. It has put together data going back to 2008 on detention by location, which it lets you download from its Github site by state.


Stateline.org analysis
Tim Henderson at Stateline.org is often the source of local reporters’ arrest analyses – his stories after each of the data releases are accompanied by a downloadable dataset that went into the analysis.


#Detention kills
Andrew Free, an Atlanta immigration attorney and activist, tracks deaths in DHS custody .

title: Stories from the Deportation Data Project
text:
In December, Albert Sun at The New York Times (gift link) found that immigration crackdowns in Los Angeles, Chicago, Washington and Massachusetts resulted in even fewer people arrested by ICE had criminal convictions than the nationwide average, and less than 10 percent of them nationwide had violent convictions. That finding mirrored stories from Texas, Charlotte (gift link) and Los Angeles along with smaller jurisdictions like Mission Local’s coverage in Northern California and the Idaho Capital Sun.
The Guardian had a different question: How often was the ICE keeping detainees in holding facilities meant for stays less than 12 hours? It found that these 170 short-term holding facilities around the country routinely violated the original 12-hour limit, and some violated a new limit of three days.
Some reporters have been able to tease out patterns of particular importance in their areas, such as The City’s analysis, with researcher James Gunther, of people arrested on their way out of the New York City immigration courthouse. The Chicago Tribune analyzed book-ins at l;local initial holding facilities during the Midway Blitz late in 2025 to encompass arrests by agencies other than ICE.
Some stories have focused on local law enforcement’s cooperation with ICE, such as Suncoast Searchlight’s analysis of detainers in Florida, or the University of Maryland’s Howard Center stories on a few rural sheriffs becoming responsible for many of the arrests across the state.
In Ventura County, reporters took a different approach: Follow people arrested during one high-profile raid on a local marijuana farm, using DDP data to fill out some of the information.
The pages that follow lay out how you can do stories like this in your area using the data and advice from the reporters.
If you need more inspiration, scroll through the stories at the DDP site – and send them links to your own stories when you publish.

title: ICE Data Primer
text:
The data collected by the DDP fall under four general categories:

Arrests: These are the easiest records to understand, but lack the geographic specificity that many local reporters would need. It’s particularly difficult to do state level trend analysis, because about 10 percent of the records didn’t record any state until about July 2025. We are providing some other hints to finding arrests in your area.
Detentions: On the other end of the spectrum are detentions, which is a table containing one row for each time a detainee is booked into a new facility. Many detainees are moved four or five times before being released, or are detained, released and re-detained. Without care, you risk counting people multiple times for the same arrest.
Detainers: The federal government can ask local law enforcement to hold people in their jails past their scheduled release so that ICE can come pick them up. These are “detainers”. Some states, like California, bar local law enforcement from cooperating with ICE – the so-called “Sanctuary Cities”. Others REQUIRE cooperation with ICE, such as Texas, Florida and North Carolina. Still others, like Maryland, leave it up to the local authorities.
Removals: These are people sent back to their home countries or to third countries in the case of asylees or others in danger. (Information on the status of a detainee or arrestee is included in some of the other tables, but it’s not as complete as the removals table would be if it were accurate.) For now, this table isn’t available.

There is one other table produced by ICE that seemd enticing but turned out to have very little of use. The encounters data is supposed to log every encounter made by ICE, whether or not it ended in an arrest. But it contained virtually no information.

title: Local arrests
text:
Get your local data
Some of the most common stories in local news outlets examine the growth of arrests by ICE and the failure of the federal government to focus mainly on convicted criminals. Across the country, reporters have found that few of the people arrested have violent convictions, and less than half have any criminal history at all. yourself.
Some other stories include:
This story is more difficult than it might seem. The arrest data provided by ICE has several problems:
That said, local reporters have been able to overcome these obstacles in a number of ways. McGlade, for example, downloaded all of the rows for one of the 25 “area of responsibility” regions – the one that includes North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia – scoured the landmark information to isolate those in and around Mecklenberg County. (This guide will show you one strategy for doing this in a Google Sheet without the need for computer programming). You can use this strategy using the data provided directly by the Deportation Data Project.
Big Local News has taken another approach: Most people arrested are taken to an ICE detention holding or intake center, which is often within a few hours’ drive of the arrest location. We have added the first detention location’s county to the enhanced data, giving you a little more information on where it likely happened. In addition, local jails are asked to hold potential immigration violators until ICE can come pick them up if they were arrested on a local charge such as a DUI. These jails are, in turn, the location of those arrests. For arrests stemming from these detainers, we have added that location to the arrest data.
The DDP has a slicer that lets you look for specific kinds of arrests and download the results, but it’s a little difficult to use for the purpose of getting arrests in your area. Instead, this guide shows you how to use the data downloaded from Big Local News, which includes the enhanced geographic information described above and simplifies the information for the purpose of reporting on arrests. This means we’ve eliminated some of the columns that might not be useful, simplified some of the categories, and lost some other details from the original data in favor of making it easier to use.

title: Appendix A — About the data
text:
Follow up from symposium of reporters
The Deportation Data Project has a detailed codebook explaining the project’s understanding of each element of the data. But the government has refused to answer questions about how it is collected, compiled and extracted. Many of its internal forms are unavailable publicly.
We have to rely, instead, on our understanding based on previous iterations of the data, former employees and the experience of journalilsts and researchers. We encourage you to let us know if your ground reporting can clarify or correct any of the questions or misunderstandings inherent in undocumented data.
Additionally, ICE seems to have randomly decided which columns to include in each table, even though all of the common elements should be available. For example, one obvious story would be the number of local people who have been in the country for decades are being arrested, versus relative newcomers; whether people arrested have legal permanent residence status, or whether they have temporary protected status. But those columns are only available in the removals table – they’re missing in the arrests, detentions and detainer data. 1
We have added insights from others’ reporting where we could in this book.
In June, Berkeley Journalism and a few other places hosted a symposium of reporters, experts, etc. to discuss immigration reporting. Our contact there is Andrés Cediel, a documentarian with a lot of interest in immigration issues. We spoke with him on Oct 10. They want to make the data more transparent, and are focused on visualizations that could be embedded. Others who are still involved include Mark Lima of CBS and (I think) Lourdes Duarte from Chicago WGN.
Their inspiration was the COVID tracking project from the Atlantic.
His story ideas were pretty straightforward: US citizens getting caught up in raids, looking at children , those without criminal records. They are working with the Berkeley-based California News Fellowship (the group that is funded by the Calif. government to fill holes in local reporting.)
Ryan explained our model of working with a national outlet to do a story that we can help get localized by partners that we’ve worked with before, then have training materials, cleaned data, etc. to provide to anyone once we know what we’re doing. In a followup note, Andrès still seemed focused on dashboard / visualizations, but Ryan clarified that.
He mentioned that LAT did a good job using the data after their protests.
We had a followup conversation with them about where the FOIAs are in DDP, and also an introduction to what we are doing, and an invitation to talk with us about it.

title: Appendix B — Arrests
text:
Definitions

ERO administrative arrests
The Deportation Data project is acquired from ICE, and refers to “ERO administrative arrests”.
In his series “A close look at ICE arrest data..”, Austin Kocher says that the Deportation Data Project’s arrest data is actually administrative arrests reported by ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations. This excludes CBP, HSI, and non-administrative arrests, he says. It suggests it excludes people caught up in protests or arrested without immigration orders.
Generally, ICE’s ERO arrests people with civil immigration law violations - they’re based on administrative arrest warrents. A CRS report says they can make arrests in two instances when they don’t have a warrant: 1) The alien is attempting to enter the country, 2) the officer has “reason to believe” the immigrant is here unlawfully and will escape if not arrested.
This second exception suggests that ICE just has to say, “I think you’re here unlawfully” and they can arrest without a warrant. These are the brief stops now called “Kavanaugh stops” because he said that using a broad definition here, even racial profiling, can fall under that exception.


Apprehension method
Generally, people have tried to distinguish arrests that came from some kind of detention from those that happened in the wild. Different groups have done it differently:

Cato Institute
The defined street arrests as:

any arrest not in state or local custody, a jail, prison, police department, office, court, detention center, or other facility.) had a piece on street vs. custody arrests, and they broke each of the 27 different kinds of apprehensions into those two categories. See the lookup tables for the exact translation. Almost all of the “From detention” are from state, local or federal jails and prisons.

It wasn’t clear how they translated the categories, and they haven’t responded to my outreach.


Other stories
LAT, the City and others have distinguished between “street arrests” and others, but they’ve used different definitions.


ICE itself
I am using the categorization suggested by the 2024 ICE annual report, page 15:


At-large arrests, which take place within the community (i.e., outside of jails or prisons).
Custodial arrests, which take place in the confines of a jail or prison, as CAP works with federal, state and local law enforcement partners to take custody of removable noncitizens who have already been arrested by another law enforcement agency for criminal activity

title: Appendix B — Arrests
text:
Handling duplicates
There are several types of duplicates, and I’m handling them in different ways. Generally,

If there is no id code for the person, I NEVER count it as a duplicate. There’s no way to tell if two people from the same country of the same age were arrested at the same time, or if it’s the same person twice.
If the same person is arrested more than once within 24 hours, I count the earlier one as a duplicate. This could concievably happen, but it would be weird.
If the same person is arrested twice at the same time, I count the one that comes first in the dataset as the duplicate. This could be wrong, and it can end up losing some data in a small number of rows.

There are other arrests, detentions and removals that are of the same person, but not duplicates – they appear to actually have been arrested or removed twice, for example. I’m keeping those, but noting which one is the last one logged.

title: Appendix B — Arrests
text:
Data questions


Clarify how much and what is missing from the ICE administrative arrest data. Kocher says it’s “likely” that it does not additional arrests. Is that true? (Hint: there are no U.S. citizens in the arrest data.)
Is it at all possible that the large number of missing final order dates refer to people who don’t have final orders of removal? If so, why are they arrested? (Possible answer: they were never documented entry, so they can be removed without a hearing?)
How are children handled in practice? I know the data here excludes OSS (HHS) detentions, but what happens in the arrest data? It’s been suggested that the ones in our data are most likely families, but there are also some in juvenile detention facilities. I think we’ll have to figure this out as people do more reporting. I think the Marshall project may have figured some of this out: https://www.themarshallproject.org/2025/12/17/children-immigration-detention-dilley-ice

title: Appendix C — Common elements used across tables
text:
Other documentation
The deportation data project posts five datasets: encounters, arrests, detainers, detentions, and removals. They also have a list of offices scraped from the sub-office website of ICE.
In the data/raw folder, I’ve made an exact copy of the data that the project posts. (Most recent in most cases.) There is also a copy that I can use for hand-editing, with more descriptive data names. That’s in the data/processed folder, even though it’s raw.
The project is pretty good about doing basic vetting of the datasets when they arrive. For example, it immediately post the removals data from July, when they found a serious flaw. They also post when each dataset is usable as history.
The data originally is extracted from DHS’s Enforcement Integrated Database, or EID, which is the back end to the department’s ENFORCE application. It’s supposed to hold details on the entire enforcement infrastructure, and is supposed to contain information from all of the enforcement agencies (I think).
The original data was downloaded from the Deportation Data Project, as of Oct. 13, 2025 (the date of this documentation). I’ll update it when they get a new batch. I downloaded the original, not cleaned, data.
There are some things to remember about all of the datasets, and some specific to individual ones.
crumbs: C  Common elements used across tables

title: Appendix C — Common elements used across tables
text:
Data cleaning checks

Duplicates
True duplicates (every column exactly the same) are removed. But there are other types of duplication that are handled table-by-table. In some cases, they actually aren’t duplicates – they refer to more than one thing happening to a person or a case. In others, they’re artifacts of a relational system and how they’re handled depends on what the substantive question is. In still other cases, they may be duplicates, but we’re not sure.
Generally:

Duplicates across all fields, including missing values. Just save one – it doesn’t matter which.
Dupes created by the relational nature of the data. For example, a person could be arrested twice, or they will show up over and over in the detention data. In each dataset, we can decide how to handle them for the purpose of local reporting. Using the same example in detention, for example, might mean that we want to create a snapshot for each detention location that has anyone who was ever in that area. For arrests, we may only want to keep the most recent OR we may want to create some summaries of arrests, and summaries of people, separately.
Dupes that appear to be the same, but have different information. An example is an arrest record that differs in most cells, but has the same unique person ID and the same date and time as others. One answer is to look at the order that the file came in, and choose the one that appears to be the most recent (top or bottom of list in their original order), or see whether one of the values suggests it is a record that SHOULD be deleted (entered in error).



Missing unique identifiers
ICE is supposed to provide a scrambled unique identifier for each person but there are quite a few missing.


Dates and times
In each table, I checked to see if there is a meaningful time element to the date. If not, I converted the original column from date-time to just date. How this gets handled by others depends on the data processing software they use. If there is a meaningful time, then I added a column with the original name and the suffix _part

title: Appendix D — Data enhancements
text:
Final program
Many of the categories used in the ICE data exist across more than one table. Definitions that only exist on one table are included in the documentation for that area. You can see which variables are in which tables on the Deportation Data Project site’s documentation.
Use the apprehension method field instead of final program to find the way that someone was actually arrested.
The final program refers to the program that ICE officers are assigned to. They may be imprecise because the officer is temporarily detailed. title: Appendix D — Data enhancements
text:
Case status and category codes
The case status and category codes contain remnants of the law as it existed before 1996, and have been constantly updated piecemeal. That makes them really difficult to understand. I’ve tried to combine and rename these codes into meaningful groups.
Although they mean different things, the case status and category tend to go together. In arrests, for example, they have the exact same number of missing values.






Warning



I still need to run these by an expert – use with care.



Case status
At the highest level, refers to whether it is in ICE’s purview. Anything that is ACTIVE is still on their books. Everything else is a reason that they’re not. I’ve grouped ACTIVE with the missing values to create “Active case”, and then grouped the 13 more detailed reasons into more general categories. The recodes are called case_status_bln in the tables.

Case category
Case category is the detailed legal reason that they are seeking removal – it doesn’t refer to what has happened in the case. I’m leaving this out of our analysis – it’s pretty complicated, and I don’t think most people care about the detailed legal reason.


Most serious criminal codes


Most serious crime categories


Decide how to deal with crime codes so they’re collapsed into meaningful categories that would be able to be used in a sentence.




Can we say that someone was only convicted of immigration offenses if that is the most serious crime? How can we characterize that?


It’s really unclear what is considered the “most serious” crime. In particular, it’s unclear whether any immigration offense, such as illegal entry, is considered more serious than, say, a DUI.

TRAC, at some point, got a list of offense codes from DHS that lists the ‘level’ of each crime, as 1, 2, or 3. We can see there that illegal entry to the US is the lowest crime category. But it doesn’t really help within the levels. (These were based on the old Morton memo, and haven’t been in use for a long time, I don’t think.)
The American Immigration Council examined the “Most serious charge” in the Criminal Alien Program that gives some detail on what they consider more and less serious.
USCIS has a list of aggravated felonies on its website, but I’m not sure how up to date it is.) (You can also be deported for crimes of “moral turpitude”.)
The ICE custody worksheet suggests that the most serious crime conviction is based on the sentence, and nothing else: https://www.ice.gov/doclib/detention-standards/2011/2-2.pdf

Also from the American Immigration Council, a description of what “aggravated felony” means:

“Aggravated felony” is a term of art used to describe a category of offenses carrying particularly harsh immigration consequences for noncitizens convicted of such crimes. Regardless of their immigration status, noncitizens who have been convicted of an “aggravated felony” are prohibited from receiving most forms of relief that would spare them from deportation, including asylum, and from being readmitted to the United States at any time in the future.
Despite what the ominous-sounding name may suggest, an “aggravated felony” does not require the crime to be “aggravated” or a “felony” to qualify. Instead, an “aggravated felony” is simply an offense that Congress sees fit to label as such, and today includes many nonviolent and seemingly minor offenses.
…
As initially enacted in 1988, the term “aggravated felony” referred only to murder, federal drug trafficking, and illicit trafficking of certain firearms and destructive devices. Congress has since expanded the definition of “aggravated felony” on numerous occasions, but has never removed a crime from the list. Today, the definition of “aggravated felony” covers more than thirty types of offenses, including simple battery, theft, filing a false tax return, and failing to appear in court.

The most serious conviction code is shown in detention, removal and detainer; the most serious charge code is in detainers.
These refer to sections of the NCIC2 , with one major omission: The NCIC codes are supposed to be suffixed with “general applicability” codes, such as “Attempt” or “conspiracy” so that the person looking at the charge would know it isn’t the substantive charge. But these are not shown in the ICE data – they are treating all of them the same way.
There are worksheets in state courts to determine the “most serious” charge codes (they differ depending on the state code), but they are generally created using the longest possible sentence. They aren’t supposed to be just any charge within a case or a person. In practice, I’ve found a couple of things: First, simple immigration crimes such as re-entry are usually only shown when there is nothing substantively more serious. Second, drug offenses are problematic: many don’t distinguish between possession and distribution (it just doesn’t say either way), so there’s no real way to know if it’s someone caught with some marijuana for personal use, or if it’s a cocaine trafficker.
We don’t have a good way to check whether or not there are other, more serious, crimes that the person was involved in. But these have historically been used to show that the government was targeting really serious criminals and it’s in their interest to have them conform to what the public thinks of as “serious”.
The “aggravated felon” categorization is a legal one: Congress decides which crimes to include in aggravated felonies for the purpose of deportation, and some of them don’t seem that bad (such as prostitution). Crimes of moral turpitude can be aggravated felonies even if they’re neither aggravated nor felonies. Most of the lesser offenses that are included in the list are limited to something with at least a one-year sentence as punishment, and often exclude crimes committed solely for a child or spouse.

title: Appendix E — Understanding the immigration enforcement system
text:
History of some of the fields
I’m not going to go into much detail here, but it’s worth understanding a few key things about how the immigration removal system works.
There are two main agencies within the Department of Homeland Security that deal with illegal immigration. Customs and Border Patrol, or CBP, only operates within 50 miles of an international border, including the coastline. The people they deal with are usually those who have crossed the border illegally, not those who have presented themselves at the border and requested asylum.
The other agency is Immigration and ? Enforcement, or ICE. They operate in the interior of the country and are responsible for cases that have already been heard by an immigration court judge. Immigration court is completely separate from the U.S district court or a state criminal court – it is staffed by Justice Department employees, not people who work for an independent judiciary. Its only job is to determine whether or not someone should be “removed”, or sent back to their home countries or, in rare cases, some other country.
Both ICE and CBP can arrest people, but they are brought to immigration, not criminal, courts and are detained by ICE, not the US Bureau of Prisons. (The people arrested may also face charge in criminal court brought by a US attorney, but that is not really part of the immigration system).
People come to the removal system in several different ways:
If an immigration judge has decided that someone should be removed, they become part of the immigration docket.
Each of these situations is obviously a little different, but the data compiled by the Deportation Data Project generally only refers to people ICE has had some contact with , and usually only who that appear on the docket. The officers can go out looking for people who should be on their docket. They can also request cooperation from state and local authorities, or raid an area and place people on the docket who don’t have the proper authority to be here.
Here are a few resources to learn more about how the system works:
This paper from Donald Kerwin of the Center for Migration Studies explains that some of the fields are remnants of historical immigration laws. I’ll try so summarize it here as it relates to the data.

title: Appendix E — Understanding the immigration enforcement system
text:
Case categories
Before 1996, “removable non-citizens” fell into two broad categories: deportable and excludable. Deportable generally means they came into the country legally – they have been lawfully admitted by going through the immigration officer at the border. Excludable means they can be sent back without the protections of going through a deportation process. Even though the law changed substantially in 1996, the data from ICE retains this language.1
For people seeking legal status, the difference is crucial: People who are excludable, or inadmissable, have to prove they have a legal right to stay. In contrast, the government has to prove that someone is deportable.
of entry, they’ve crossed the border without being seen by an immigration officer (they snuck in), they apply to become a legal permanaent resident (green card holder), or they have been convicted of a crime and seek to be admitted sometime in the future.
At the time, immigrants who had entered the country before the 1996 law had greater rights, and were sent through deportation. But those stopped at the border became “excludable” based on the idea that they had no “entered” the country.
All of this language can be important, since it maps to the data columns provided by ICE.

Source: “Immigration Consequences of a Criminal Conviction in North Carlina”, chapter 3



Effects of criminal convictions on deportation and admission status
Most states have some sort of chart that maps the federal policy to their own criminal code, such as this one from the University of Maryland: https://www.law.umaryland.edu/media/sol/sol-2022-images-and-files/academics/programs-and-centers/chacon-center-for-immigrant-justice-program/pdfs-docs-and-files/Md-Imm-Conseq-Chart-6-15-2021-revision-FINAL.pdf

title: Appendix E — Understanding the immigration enforcement system
text:
Glossary

Admission and deportation status

Admission

Lawful entry into the U.S. after inspection and authorization by an immigration officer. INA § 101(a)(13)(A), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(A). People become “excludable” if they are in the country without proper admission.

Deportability

applies to noncitizens who have been lawfully admitted to the U.S. (even if their lawful status has expired).

Inadmissibility

applies to people who are seeking admission into the U.S. Green card holders convicted of certain crimes may not be able to return falling after traveling abroad on the grounds of inadmissibility

Excludable

Same as inadmissable, people who have not gone through the proper immigration or entry checks, including people caught within 100 miles of the border soon after arriving.




Legal proceedings
In most cases, immigration officials have to go before an immigration judge to get an order of removal. But there are several categories that avoid this step, and can result in immediate removal.
Examples include:

Expedited removal

Removing people caught within 100 miles of the border after entering illegally, and have been in the country less than 2 years. This may sound like a narrow group, but it’s huge. Every coastline is a border, making people in the largest population centers subject to expedited removal. Expedited removal traditionally was used by the Customs and Border Patrol and applied to people who just arrived. The Trump administration is using it through ICE in large cities around the country. These are sometimes called “returns”.

Reinstatement of removal

Applies to people who left either voluntarily or by being removed and re-enter illegally.

Administrative removal

Removal of people who have been convicted of an “aggravated felony”, as defined by Congress2. Aggravated felonies are not what they seem. They include crimes as serious as murder but also some people convicted of prostitution.


Pacific Enforcement Response Center (PERC) Tue, 06/12/2018 - 15:45 ICE established the PERC in January 2015 to serve as a tactical force multiplier for the Law Enforcement Support Center (LESC) and ERO field offices nationwide. Located in Laguna Niguel, California, the PERC operates round-the-clock 365 days per year and takes appropriate law enforcement action upon aliens suspected, arrested, or convicted of criminal activity across the United States. After initial alienage determination is made at the LESC, trained law enforcement officers at the PERC manage the high volume of actionable criminal leads requiring immediate enforcement action.
The PERC protects and defends the United States by sharing timely and relevant ICE information with ERO field offices and law enforcement partners nationwide, issuing immigration detainers/request for notification on high-priority and high-risk criminal aliens. The primary users of the PERC are ERO and ICE field offices that benefit from real-time enforcement decisions and actions made by the PERC. Officers at the PERC support DHS’s overarching mission to enhance national security and public safety by furthering the removal process of priority criminal aliens from the United States.
